sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: It's February 10th, 2005. My name is Tom Weiner. I'm an historian for the Veterans' History Project for the Library of Congress. And I'm interviewing Norman Portenoy today in his home, in Washington, DC.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Norman, could you spell your last name for the record, and tell us what branch of the service you were in, and what war or wars you served in?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay. I was in the, what is now the U.S. Air Force; it's the Army Air Corps, at the time; and I served through World War II, Korea, and really resigned, or didn't resign, I actually retired in 1968, having gone through the course of all these events, and to include Viet Nam, but not out there, but serving in this country in support of Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. Why don't you tell us a little bit about your life before you came into the military; where you were born, where you grew up, and your schooling.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay. I was born actually in New York City. My father was British, my mother American. When I was two years old, my parents moved to London, and obviously I went along with and was raised in London, and left there in 1941 to come back here. The reason-- my education in so far as, as my early life was at British secondary schools and to the University of London; and then left there to come back here with my parents. Now, that produces a rather interesting episode, in that in 1939, in late 1939, several, a number of my school chums with myself went down to enlist in the British Service. It was our intention to save Great Britain from all that was going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This is in 1939, when Britain entered the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Britain entered the war, and the war was going on, and we went in because we thought that it was time for us to save Great Britain. So, we did. It was seven of us at the time, and a little team went down there to enlist. Six of them immediately enlisted without any problem. And when they got to me, they said we may have a little delay, possibly a week or two at the most, because you're a dual citizen, and we have to get through that portion of the problem. And I said, okay, fine. They said, but we will get to you very quickly. I went back home, and my school chums all got themselves, after a couple of weeks, they were pretty deeply involved. And I wandered around doing nothing, waiting for them to call me. It got to the point where I was pretty, pretty annoyed about all this. I felt that I should have gotten in there with my friends. And then, a peculiar circumstance, about--after I'd been doing this for about a month and a half, my father was asked to go back to New York as part of the British purchasing commission to do some purchasing for the war effort, the British war effort. And mothers, being as they were, would not stand for me to stay there; I had to come back with them. So, I came back to this country. And we settled in New York, where my father was doing his job. And I wandered around in the suburbs of New York for about a month, until I got to the point where I was beginning to get very upset. Nothing was happening, and everybody was doing everything, and I had nothing to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: How old were you at this time?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: At that time, I was--oh, in 1939, I was 19. I was 19, then, and I was ready to do something constructive. Anyway, this went on for a while. Finally, I said that's, that's it. So, I went down to the enlistment people in New York City, and I enlisted in the Army Air Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Why the Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, I was--I wanted -- had I got in the British Service, I would have been in the British Service flying. Of course, not that I was a pilot by nature, but I had been involved in all sorts of things that are peripheral to that sort of thing; car, automobile racing, and things like that, which I was fond of. Besides, I was fascinated to fly. So, as I say, I finally went down and enlisted in the Army Corps. And they said we will, we will call you shortly, you know; we'll get you going.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This is in--now we're 1940, or are we still in '39?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Now, we're well into '40. We're actually getting close, we're getting close to '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. So, it's late, late '40?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Late '40.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Then came Dunkirk, you will recall, and -- or no. Or, no. Pearl Harbor, that was -- then came. Then we were, then we were in the war. At which point, they called me immediately. And I went off to flying school. I think it was just about, as I recall, it was very close the beginning of '41. Or actually it was late '40, getting ready, and then--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, Pearl Harbor was December of '41.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Okay--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- when that happened, I was, about a week later, I was called.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. So, you're entering into the Service in December or January?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah; end of December.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay, end of December '41?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That's right, '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Where did you go for your training?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: My first exposure to flying school was in Arcadia, Florida. A primary flying school, little aircraft. And I spent three, four months learning to fly the light aircraft there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Had you ever flown before?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No, not as a--not as a pilot, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: But you had--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I'd been--oh, I'd been in an airplane --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- but you had been in an airplane?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- many times. But, but not as a pilot. And this what started me out with training on this aircraft, a PT-17, I think they called it. A little two wings, a little, small aircraft, which they did their primary flying on for everybody. So, I did that for a couple of months and then graduated from that to, to the next layer up, which was at Montgomery, Alabama, as a matter of fact, at Gunter Field Air, where you got into the first aircraft that looked like it might be a fighter, in that the it was a low-reign aircraft, and so on. So, I took a further advanced flying there for another several months. And then I was graduated there and sent to a final advanced flying school in Dothan, Alabama, as a matter of fact , as I remember it. And there I completed my fly training as a fighter pilot. That's where you graduated with all the tactics that you could. And from there I was sent to a flying training, a tactical fighting school, to learn to fly a particular fighter like the F-40 or whatever it is. I got there and I started my training, and I was called into the Commander's office. And he said, you and--he named two other guys -- have been selected. We want you to -- where the Army Air Corps is going into heavy aircraft flying. And we're providing people who we think can pick up the ability to fly large aircraft to begin training. So, he said, so, you and these other guys will go now to get the training as you might call heavy transport pilots.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. So, you were out of the fighting business?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Out of fighting and into heavy transport.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And he said, now, and you will report for duty, he said, pack your bag and day after tomorrow you report for duty in Atlanta, Georgia, to Eastern Airlines. I said, Eastern Airlines? Yes, Eastern Airlines. There you will learn how to fly transport. They will teach you. So, I reported there. And sure enough, day and night, I flew with their various airline captains and pilots and--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you were flying in a commercial aircraft?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was flying in a commercial aircraft that they had on the ground at the time, which they used for training their own men, as well as the commercial. So, I did that for two months. I flew day and night. And finally one day, the captain that I was flying with said, okay, tonight be here at 6:00 because you are going to start flying as if you were a captain on Eastern Airlines. You're going to fly from Atlanta to New York. And your take-off is going to be midnight. And you will fly and stop at the following places, which was about five or six places. And he said, and I'll be watching what you do. I'll be your co-pilot, and go where I say. So, I did that, and it was, it was an interesting experience, I should say. And--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Were you nervous?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Not nervous, but cautious. You know, you're not sure what you're up against. But it happened to have been a reasonably good weather that night, as I remember. Otherwise, I really would have had a problem. But it was, it was good. It was something you could get, really get to, you know. It was the real thing; you were not just practicing. So, I flew. And I remember we went from Atlanta to, to Charlotte, North Carolina, and Richmond, and all the rest of them, and into New York City. I did that for one month. About every third night they'd get me up and we would fly that same route. About the end of that, again I got a visit into the office of the Commander. He said, now, we're going to transfer you for further training in this kind of thing to United Airlines in Denver, Colorado. And he said, now, you're going to learn here not how to fly the airplane, but how to navigate in places where there's nothing to navigate with. You're supposed to be able to learn how to handle your airplane and kind of consciously figure how you might get from one place to another without having any great vehicle to show you or teach you, or let you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Well now, when you say without--without any instruments?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Or without any--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well no. Without--without instrument aids. Without ground aids to -- like, like lights, or the -- all the various things on the ground; farmhouses, roads, lakes, things like that. You have to learn how you can use that to go from here or there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure. So, kind of flying blind, in a way?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It is. In a sense, you would be able to keep your aircraft in the air, but if you didn't know where you were going, it wouldn't have made much difference, you know. So, this was the, this was the approach that they gave me at united. So, the captain there began training me on how to look out over terrain, how to judge distance, things, time, you know. And, and how to draw a line with a direction on it, and what you want to achieve, and how to watch whether you're getting closer or nearer, that sort of thing. Well, a technique which you would use, and did use considerably, once you get out into the world where they don't have anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, I did that for about a month, a little over a month, about a month and a half, probably. And then I got the same call again. And they said, okay, now you've got the idea, you're doing okay, and that's fine. Now we're transferring you to operational duty. You will report to--I forgot what the number of the squadron was -- at LaGuardia Field. And so, I arrived there. And I found that this was a very small outfit. And it was the Special Mission Squadron, which is where we began, at LaGuardia Field.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, what does the Special Mission Squadron do?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It is designed primarily to fly important people, the President. We fly Air Force One, Air Force Two, and take anybody, any of them of rank or consequence, wherever in the world they had to go. That's what this squadron was designed to do. And now, it was, it was assembled in an interesting fashion. It was, there were approximately, I believe, at most times six or seven airline captains who had been brought in, who were Reserve, who had among them--they were bringing, training, specialized flying for years, had -- none of them had under ten thousand hours. Some of them had even twice that amount. They were old heads; very, very experienced. And they were the senior pilots. And then, there were--we had had six or seven of them. And then we had six or seven junior pilots who would serve as first pilot before the captain. And then we had a seconds first pilot who was even less experienced than the first pilot. You know, in other words, it was kind of a thing. Plus, training navigators who were not from an airline, but the highly trained ones being captains and first lieutenants and even a major or two. But the whole squadron consisted of about--well, eight or nine of us junior, second pilots, seven first pilots, and about three or four navigators. And then the mechanic-engineers and stuff, plus three stewards, GIs who served as.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That was, that was the squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, how many planes were involved in this?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Then, we had--we started out with about -- well, available to us as we may need it, four or five, various depending on it, of C-47's. And then with about four or five Dc-4's, four-engine. And then we had a couple of spare Lockheed Lone Stars that they added for us to work with locally or whatever we wanted. So, that was the total range of our equipment. We had on call, if we needed it, almost any airplane in the country. But that was our regular crew with which we got used to in flying, flying it. And we did not fly as set crews. We were, we were put together as it may be needed. You know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I see. So, you were interchangeable parts?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We were all, we were all interchangeable.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Let's back up for a second, because I want to get into what your missions were.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: But what I want to do is back up a little bit and talk about your adjustment to military life.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What was it like? Did you like being in the military? How was the barracks life like for you; the food, the comradery, the situations you were in on a day-to-day basis?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, let me--I suppose I'm going to sound weird. But the group and the relationships that we had were to me quite acceptable. Yes, here and there, there were a couple of chintzy guys who, not because they were fundamentally chintzy, but because they'd never seen anything quite like they were facing. And rather than trying to get in it, they tried to get out of it. Which was -- they were very few and far between. The treatment. If you were--if you were used to meals either at your home or at a lovely restaurant, you might find it a little difficult to get along. Because they did solid, good food; they did all right; you never -- you didn't suffer, but it was not exactly spectacular. On the other hand, with the group there was always something going on, there was always something that you could kid about or talk about. And also, the war was picking up, and we were getting inputs from all over about what was happening. And you tried to apply that to how you would fit and what you would do, and that sort of thing; you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, it was not--let's say it was, it was not what you'd want to do for a lifetime. On the other hand, if you had to do it and you liked to fly, you enjoyed handling that stuff, this was a good compliment. It did help you. You didn't a starve. You weren't hungry. You had a bunch of guys, some of them you thought were a little, a little short on a lot of things. A lot of them were good country boys. A few of them; not a lot, a few of them. Because the selection of people it brought were all, with some experience and some savoir-faire, they had to be able to handle themselves in this kind of a climate. They knew why they were getting us. We didn't know what, or what we were going to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Because from--for a long time you were being groomed for this, but they weren't telling you what you were being groomed for?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, that was, that was--Yeah, that's exactly it. There was no -- that wasn't even mentioned. And you, you -- by the time you finished going to a primary and, and then you got into these other ones, you had a cross-section of experience which you would never equate anywhere else. There was no way you assemble it like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, you had a good cross-section going from very primary to very sophisticated work. And by the time we were shipped to the squadron, we were not--had not been used in a sophisticated fashion, but we had been trained as if we were in a sophisticated group. And so, it was interesting. And those of us who did go had demonstrated, prior to that, that we did like what we were doing. You know, that we enjoyed the flying and the comradery, if you will. And we recognized that some guys were not going to make it. But that's the way, you know --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: You win some, you lose some, and you get rained out a lot. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. So, you were stationed at LaGuardia starting when?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Starting--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- the latter part of '41. The middle to latter part of '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: No, '41 is when you went in.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: --into '42, about the middle of '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you're saying probably '42 to '43. Because--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, I was--I was still -- in '42, I was into LaGuardia. Because then, we were there only a short time, then we moved down here.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. Out here, being where?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: What's the name? Here. This field. Nashville.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh, Nashville?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you were--so, you were started out at LaGuardia?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We started at LaGuardia.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: But then they moved you to--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: They moved the whole operation out of LaGuardia to here, to Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And here to --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Wasn't National Airport fairly new then?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, let's put it this way. It was not as sophisticated as it is now, but it didn't have the traffic that it has now.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We had two hangars. And we had a building behind--which is one of the buildings that are still there, but they were a little bit more primitive. And that served us for, you know, for training, for piloting, for assembling and so forth. And we flew out of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Where did you live?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I got a little apartment in, in Virginia, here. Down, just down--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: In Arlington?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, in Arlington. Actually, on the road, the--gosh, I can't remember names anymore. But the main road that goes down, past the --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: On Route 1?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, it wasn't Route 1; it was the parkway that went down that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh. Like the George Washington Parkway?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, like that. And when you get down there about a couple of miles, the apartments, small apartments that are along the edge there. And so, I had a little apartment there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And that was, like, near the river you mean?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well, it was -- yeah. It was, it was the parkway, and then there was a bit of stuff growing there, and then the river. And I was up that side of the river.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, the pentagon was under correction then?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you see it being built?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, I mean, yeah, it was going on. Yeah, you could see it, I mean. But we didn't have anything to do with that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You didn't have anything--you didn't go there at all?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. No, that was not--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you just went between your apartment and the airport?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And the airport, which had our meeting place and our training and everything else was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We didn't have any other place to go.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: All right. So, now what were what was your first--do you remember your first mission on the Special Missions group?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Actually, the first special missions, I don't remember precisely. But the first special missions were domestic. They were flying general officers into training camps to look at somebody; flying to another headquarters command; flying to San Francisco to, to put them in someplace like that. And we did that for a while. I say a while. We flew constantly. So, you know, it wasn't as if you were sitting around there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I was going to say. What was your routine? Was there a daily routine? Or was it just you were on call all the time?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, we were on call all the time. And our routine was that if you got--you were, I think, reasonably fortunate, at that point, to get three or four days off after a trip out for three or four days a week. But you also had a lot of short ones. They would call you the next day, go from here go up to New York, or go to a short, some local place; take somebody who had to have a meeting, and you took them. So, we flew a good, a good 80 hours a month.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Eighty hours a month?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Easy. Yeah. For the first couple months. But now, after you've been flying for, like, a long period of time, then they began to look at you maybe for number two pilot to the senior captains. So, there was a two--there was a two and a three, officers. So, after about a month and a half or two months of doing short ones, some of which I was put on as a first pilot because they were smaller aircraft, DC-3's and so forth, and it was, it was not any distance. But then, when we got to the big ones, whether it was to domestic or to overseas, when they had to bring the captains, big captains on, then you were on the road a lot. And they made sure you knew what you were doing. You know, that kind of thing. So, I began a couple overseas, a couple overseas flights began about three months after I was down here at the field. And that began with a trip overseas. First couple of them--well, to London.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Do you remember who you took to London?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Probably.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I mean, a military person or?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, it was--it was a general.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I didn't need the name. I was just kind of curious if--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- if you knew it?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- the first several trips were with one or two--the first two trips with were to London and where else -- London, to Paris, I -- no, I don't know about Paris.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I don't think you could have flown into Paris yet.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No, I didn't go to Paris. We were not ready then. London and let's see, where else.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Would you have been able to fly to Africa?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That, I was going to say. No, the first time I came through Africa was when we went to Yalta, coming back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Coming back from Yalta?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well, that was a--the trip to Yalta --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Let's talk about that. You did go to--you did fly somebody to the Yalta Conference, right?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yalta Conference, we flew what's his name.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: The Secretary of State?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, Stenttinius.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Stenttinius.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: All right, Stenttinius and his entire staff.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh. And they were on your plane?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: They were, yes. They came. We flew as Air Force Two. Air Force One was ahead of us, the President. And we flew as Air Force Two. And in fact I flew many more trips as Air Force Two, then. But we took Stenttinius and his--and all of his legendary people, the people that he needed for the conference and meetings and stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, how many planes were in this group that were flying over to Yalta?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: To Yalta, here were only the two.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you have any escort?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. We had--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Really? You were on your own?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. We had the President's One and Air Force Two, ourselves. And there were no other aircraft in that entourage, in that business. Now, there were a couple of aircraft that arrived subsequent to our arrival from various parts. Some was--one, that's one out of the States, and a couple out of Africa or somewhere else, to attend meeting. And they were usually all officers, general officers with one or two staff. Or they were some--one of them had technicians, technical people, that they thought would be of assistance. The State Department people coming were also some, a couple of technical, in the sense that they understood the name of the game, how to, how to--what they were doing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Were you concerned about being attacked or shot down in this kind of a situation?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. Well.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did it ever occur to you that--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. Well, first of all--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- the Germans might come after you?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Not really. The course that we took would have made it difficult for anybody to get at us.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We flew from Washington, out of Washington, and we went around through the Mediterranean, and into -- the Russians had a way that we were required to follow in order to do this.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh. They set the flight pattern?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: They set--once we got to Russia.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Our flight paths was to Russia; was our own until we got there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And then they--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: But, when we got to Russia, we were going to be--had to be flying in from the very down south, very way out, and into a town called Poltava. Now, Poltava is almost a direct line north to Moscow. And Poltava is a field which you can get at pretty easy and it could take DC-4's, C-54's.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Big enough.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And so, our--the Russians had done this. Subsequently, they did it several times. They had -- that was their rule. If you wanted to get into Moscow, or what have you, you would go to Poltava, and they would guide you. Now, as with this one, we came to Poltava, and they gave us Russian navigator and a Russian radio operator to sit up with us and guide us up to Moscow. And we land in Moscow, and then they were gone. But that was the way that they did that. And that will be interesting to you in can subsequently when I point out something else that we did. But that's how we got to Moscow. And any other aircraft that went in, it was One, Two, ourselves and any other, went to Poltava and then came up, and the Russian kept track of how we went and where you went and how--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, they very tightly controlled everything?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yes. Everything. They knew exactly what you were supposed to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: How long were you in Yalta?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: A week.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What did you do while you were there? It must have been kind of boring.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Nothing. Mostly wander around very, in a very small circle.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I imagine your access to anything was pretty limited, right?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No, there was nothing to do. So, you do a little reading and you play a little cards. And we talked a little bit, around and about. People came in and out to talk, see us for, for one thing or another. We spent a lot of time at the aircraft, making sure that it was in shape. But, that was about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you--did you have any access to news about what was going on at the conference?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Not particularly. No. That was not our business. You know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: There was no--there was -- we got no outcome during the course of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We got a little out of it after, when we started leaving and was on the way back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: On the way back--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did they--did they talk about what had happened?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. See, then they would, they kind of went through a little bit with us. But we had more excitement to take care of then than we had going in.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And why was that?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Because Stenttinius sat down, when he got to the end of his meeting, and he said to Bill, the senior pilot and my myself, we sat down, and he said, now, I want to visit, see a few places, since I'm here, to get a feel for what's going on. He said, so, I will tell you where I'd like to go and you guys take me there. They were on our way back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay. So, what can that be? Well, first he went--we took him to Liberia. He wanted to meet the President of Liberia, who was an American, if you remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure, yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay. So, we spent a day to there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This was not on the schedule?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. This was--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This was a surprise?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: None of the--no, nobody knew where in the hell -- well, they knew where we were, because we kept in communication.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: But that was nothing to do with schedule. That was what he thought would be useful to him. You know, sort of like, since I happen to be out in the street here, I might as well.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And Roosevelt went on ahead back?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, he went directly back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, we arrived after Yalta, and then we went to Liberia, to Monrovia. And we visited with the President there. And we were taken on little, little tiny tours; you know, come look at this city, you know, stuff that meant a great deal to us. You know, we were highly emotional about that. But, well, you know, you had to do something. So, we finished there, and then he said, okay, now I want to go to Buenos Aires. So, the next thing is we tooled up, and then we went to the Azores, and into Buenos Aires with him; took him in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: That's a long way.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yes, it is a long haul.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And he had a good visit there, and met with the people he wanted to meet. I can't remember who it was. And we had a little time to wander around, see what was going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: That, that was probably interesting.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It was worth the trouble.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Because of--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And then from there he said, next, Mexico City. And I think, I was just looking at a picture that shows us leaving the meeting at the--at the President's place in Mexico City. We did that, and had a nice visit, and then back to Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Wow. So, how many--how long did that take, from Yalta to Washington, through all those stops?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, back into Washington, it took a couple weeks.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Because we were stopping two days, three days; you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And in those days you couldn't fly as far in a plane without stopping--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, we didn't have a ready fueling.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- for refuelling, right?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We had to refuel, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, you know, you had to stop on the way. Like, we stopped at the Ascensions to get to Buenos Aires.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I was just going to say, you can't-- you couldn't fly, in those days, from the --

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. But, Buenos Aires to Mexico City was within reach.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You could do that nonstop?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That we could do.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And Mexico City to Washington, we could make. But these are--remember, we had no load on there other than a few passengers, and so we could load all the fuel we could get. And those worked okay, in our favor. Now, you can't always do it, but you get a break sometimes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, Yalta is your, your first big adventure. I mean, you have other smaller ones.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, sure. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: But that was obviously -- I mean, that's one of the most important things in--that happened.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, those are memorable. Following that, another one following of that nature was Potsdam.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh, you flew there, too?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, we were there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, this is Stenttinius?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Same bunch.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And Truman was in the plane ahead?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: He was in the seat, there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: He was in Air Force One and you were in Two, again?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. And we followed them. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What's the origin of Air Force One? Is that when they first started calling the plane that took the President Air Force One?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: That's during World War II?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. When the squadron became essentially a real entity, and that's where you looked to for support, by all these generals and senators, and everybody that was up there that could warrant a trip.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Before then, when Roosevelt wanted to fly somewhere--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- he would just--he would just --

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: He would request an airplane.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- a regular military airplane. So, when World War II happened, they decided we need a--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Once Roosevelt made that theme, we then got aircraft that was, that was set up for him.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It had the right kinds of things inside.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Especially for the fact that he was paralyzed?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Exactly. So, they had it all set up. And the same for Air Force Two, only not so palatial.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah. Sure?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Although, it wasn't bad. In other words, it was comfortable, and comfortable enough, although it was special for the President.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What was the seating capacity on the plane you were on, do you remember --

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- how many passengers it would take?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Maybe 25.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And how many in the crew?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We had three, four, six. Six.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Six onboard?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right. They were engineers and then--and oh, seven. And a steward.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And a steward?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you flew to Potsdam?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Was there any adventure in doing that?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Coming back, either coming or going?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No, that was pretty much a standard deal out and back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: There was no unexpected stops along the way back?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. There was no--there was no request for anything more than get me back.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And was it the same deal while you were in POtsdam as in Yalta; were you bored, where there wasn't anything to do?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes. Well, it's the same thing, you know. You're in a--you land on an airfield which, when we arrive, if Air Force One and Two were there, we had practically a regimental circle around you. You, you don't -- there's nothing. Nobody gets to do anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You can't go into town and go to a nightclub or a bar or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: You, we could. But there was no incentive to do that. Because there you are, you're it, and who's going to watch; you know. You know what I mean. So, it wasn't something that you had time for. You know, you wanted to watch what you were doing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Exactly. Keep your eye on the ball.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah. So, those were the two big flights that you took. And at that point then--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, those are--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- and Potsdam--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, those are relative to that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Now, there were other ones with the generals that we went on. I'm just trying to think. General Reybold, was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: General Will Reybold.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We had, we had several generals that we would fly to various places.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Around the world?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Around--yeah, around the world. I think we took, we took somebody down to -- what did we do? We took something down to Africa. We took somebody up to, up to Scandinavia, somewhere.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This is all during the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. And these were--I had a trip with -- after Stenttinius and so on, we had a trip. There was a four-star -- he was three stars then -- four stars, Ira Acher, General Acher. You may remember the name. He became Chief of Staff of the Air Command.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: When he assume it had command, he had been in there about maybe a month at most. We got a request at the office saying I want to be, have an aircraft ready to take me to visit all of the commands. I want to talk to all the senior commanders.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This is around the world?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right. That's exactly what.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, we got ready. And in 19 days we flew him around the world, westbound.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: West?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you started from Washington?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Washington to west coast, to Hawaii, and then down into the south Pacific area. And then I remember one of the main ones that just challenged the hell out of us was that he wanted to meet General Stillwell, who was in the Burma jungle. So, he said I want to meet Stillwell and he's in the Burma jungle, and he's got a place he says you can get into with your airplane. And here's where it is. Take me. So, we went over there and we found that what they had done was cut down a lot of trees, an open place, and they put down a peer plank steel plank, you know, a foot, regular runway type thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: About six or seven thousand feet, in this jungle. And he told us that's where it was, and we were to go in there, land there, and Stillwell would meet us.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, they put this runway down just for you?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, it turned out that they had a need for it for fighters, and so--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- so, it didn't, wasn't in our honor.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, this is--the war is still going on?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yes. Stillwell's in the middle of a jungle there, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, we landed at this--this is the meeting. Because we landed there at the scene. It's kind of sweaty getting it in, getting in.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And we pulled up near the front. And Acher got up and walked to the door. We opened it, put it down. And you saw over in the corner is a card table and two chairs. So, he walked over to that, and he stood a minute. And lo and behold, Stillwell comes out of the jungle, by himself, walks over, sits down at the chair, and the two of them talk for about an hour. They shake hands. He comes back and he says, okay, let's keep going. He gets back on the airplane. From there we went--from Burma, we went, I guess, I think Italy, and to France, France to England to England, England to Bermuda, or was it -- it was Puerto Rico, and then into Washington. But he had his meeting with Stillwell. And we met, at these various places that we stopped, I don't recall them well anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you have any close shaves? Were there any times where--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- you were--how about weather?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Weather, we had plenty of weather.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That, that was a given. That's a given.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure. You never had any bad experiences like with lightening or bad storms--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- that rocked you around a little bit?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. Those, when we got ready to go, the weather could be bad, but it was flyable and acceptable. And we never kind of pushed it to see how far we could get while it was doing whatever it was doing. So, we were very fortunate. We did have -- we did have a lot of low ceilings and stuff to land in; you know. But first of all, from my point of view, the Captain, Bill Richmond was his name. He was from Northwest Airlines. He had been flying many years. He had 18,000 hours at the time he came with us. So, he had been flying a good time. And to him, weather was not a factor. I mean, he decided to go and he was use it had to seeing you it. And I had been flying, as in much I had, but flying with him, I flew in all kinds of weather, and gradually I got so I was quite comfortable flying in weather, which served me well later on, because then I was a senior pilot. But we had we had a lot of lousy weather to fly in, but none that wasn't acceptable to do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure. Now, the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I understand that you had a little adventure right after the end of the war, flying into Germany.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Let's see.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You were flying into Berlin, right?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, we did. Now, that would be a nice adventure. We were not going to Berlin. We were, we were taking, who was it, the Liaison General in Moscow was in Washington for a meeting. They called us, myself and my crew. Said, okay, he wanted, you have to get him back to Moscow as quickly as possible. So, we cranked up the airplane, got in, and we went on up to Moscow, got him to Moscow in short order, including stopping in Poltava to pick up these things, which aggravated the hell out of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did the navigator--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: But we did that. But we had to do that. But we got in there, and it was fine. He thanked us, went back to his work, and we were getting ready to leave the next morning. And before we got organized, one of his aids called and said General wants to see you guys first thing in the morning. So, the next morning we got up and got dressed and went over to the, to the embassy, which is where his office was, and reported to him, and said we're here. He said, I want to leave as soon as possible to Berlin. Have any of you seen Templehof? And smart-ass me, I say, well, General, yeah, in a sense I have. There's been a lot of bombing there, and this is a big airplane, it's 180,000 pounds. You know, you get into one of these holes and it's goodbye Charlie. He said, the Russians have assured me that everything has been filled up and it's ready.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, Templehof is what?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Templehof is a Berlin airport.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It still is, a main, one of the main airports in Berlin. Which we didn't know what the hell he had in mind. But he said, you go there, take me there, that's where I want to go.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, when is this? This is right before the end of the war or right after?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: This is a day and a half, a day and a half prior to the signing of the cease fire.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: The cease fire? Wow.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. It was May 5th, I guess we were, we were there -- yeah. They signed it on May 6th, or 7th.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: The seventh.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: The morning of the seventh. So, we were there the sixth. Yeah. We left, we left Moscow early morning of the sixth, and got into Templehof within a couple hours. We got a Russian fighter escort as far as Posnun in Poland, and then they left us. And we--if anything happened it was tough shit. It was Russian fighters anyway. So, we then got, went over to Templehof. Flew down and had a look, and couldn't see anything. And so, we landed. And as we taxied along--and Templehof, at the time, was a large grass with concrete circle outside. Not any runway, but only outside. But it was all grass for landing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. So, that made it a little worrisome. Anyway, the weather wasn't bad. When we landed and as we taxied along to where we could see there was a regimental group standing, we could see where they had put sand in the holes. And I said, Jesus, all you got to do is get your nose wheel in that, and you're, you're on your head; see. But we didn't. We were with fine. We pulled up to this group, and it turned out to be a Russian regimental band complete, standing there waiting with cars. We thought what the hell's--you know. This is weird. General got out. And -- oh, he took with him, when we went, was a British Admiral. Admiral Archer, who was the British Admiral there and liaison in Moscow. And the two of them got out. They got in the car. They got the reception there with the band. And they left. And we were just standing there; you know, like, so, what the hell do we do? So, we sat there for about a half hour, 45 minutes. Then I suddenly said--I called my radio operator. I said turn on our frequency here; see you can hear anything going on, any traffic, anything going on. So, he went up in the airplane, he turned it on. And in about five minutes he yelled out the window, yes, we've got airplanes coming from France, here. He said they're about fifteen minutes now. And it turned out that from the main headquarters in France came the British Air Vice Marshall, and all the rest of them came in two aircraft, two C-47's, came and landed. They got out, got in their cars and they left. We still didn't know what the hell we were there for. You know, just to be there. Right? So, that was, that was what we saw. Well, finally I got to the point where I, you know, I said to Bill, you know, we can stand here like a couple of dummies, but; you know. END SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE. BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: All right. We're going to pick up on the second side of the tape? Norman, you were telling me the story about being in Berlin at the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You had landed before everybody else.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We landed. We were there, just sort of sitting there, waiting. Two more aircraft came from France, which brought the other commanding officers for the forces. And they left, and we were just there. And so, finally I went to the, this leader of the Russian regimental band; you know, a captain. And he didn't speak English; he spoke obviously, I guess; but he did understand, speak some French. And my French is absolutely lousy, but it's enough to get a message across. So, I said to him, how long? He said, for what? You know. I said, well, we need quarters, we needed some place to stay overnight. He said, okay, wait. And about 20-minute later cars came up and they took us, threw us in the car and they drove us outside the airport, just outside, where there were apartment buildings. And they said, now, here is where you will stay. And there was one apartment building which they had said we would go to. We went in, and it was absolutely empty. And we went into the ground floor, and in the oven there's some food that was cooking, or that had been shut down. What they had done was completely emptied an apartment building for six of us. And, so--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: They just--they just herded everybody out --

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Just, just--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- that was living there?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- just cleared it out, because we were going to be staying there. And that's the way they wanted to do it; you know. So, they cleaned this apartment and left us there. It was, it--we got some food. And we just, we sat there. And the next morning they turned up early in the morning with the cars and brought us back to the airfield. And we still didn't know the sense of the trip, what's happening.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And about a couple hours later, suddenly, we--the cars started coming back onto the airfield. All of the things. So, we got -- we got in front of the airplane and waited, as is our custom. And the General got out of the car. And he said, okay, back to Moscow. Okay. So we got set, got into the airplane and about, oh, probably within the hour, got off the ground back to Moscow. We were in the air maybe, oh, perhaps we were in the air maybe 45 minutes on our way. And the door of the cockpit opens, and the General is up, up there. He said, I suppose you would like to know what we were doing there. And we said, well, yes, sir; sure. He said, well, you'll want to know that the war is over. He said, we just signed a cease fire.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh. He said, right. That's it. So, he said, get me to Moscow, so I can get this information out. But he said, that's what is true. The war is over in Europe. So, that was, yeah, you know, real exciting.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Well, it's, it's kind of frustrating, wasn't it, because you want to celebrate, but you have to fly the plane.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We had a couple more hours of flying.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, did you celebrate when you got to Moscow?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, we had a few cheers and a few drinks, but that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, that, that started this sequence. Because the next day we stayed, because the General didn't know what was going to be. Then he said, okay, you can go back to Washington now. So, we got ourselves all set and got everything refuelled. And that's--that's when this thing started. What we did, we said--oh, oh. The General said -- oh. I know I had, I had an important part -- Well, the next day, he, the General called us and he said I'm going to put my officer, Security Officer on board with you to go back to Washington; plus a bunch of files which he is going to take with him and file cabinets; and I want you to get back as fast as you can. So, that was interesting; you know. So, when we got ready to go, Dr. Mallory sat down and he said, okay, let's take the fastest we can. So, we agreed we were going to go, instead of the Russians taking us down to Poltava again, we went, we turned right around and went from Moscow to Preswick in Scotland, which is north instead of south. And then, from Preswick to Goose Bay which is in Newfoundland up there, and then to Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Two stops?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Two stops. And that was thirty-five hours and thirty-five minutes. That was the record.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And that was the record Moscow to Washington?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes. That was a Moscow record.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, how did you get out of Moscow without your Russian accompaniment?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, we, we said, the war is over.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Ah, so that was your excuse.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We took the position that the war is over, no time for --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: No need for--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No need for any of those special considerations.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And they accepted that?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, they were a little bit dazzled and something like all of us. You know, we didn't know how it was going to--we'd know what to do next.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, then you got to celebrate, when you got back to Washington, right?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Then when we got back to Washington, and then we really had a good one.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, were you--did you get married during the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: We got married in 1946.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh. You got married--so, did you know your wife then, when the war was over?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes. Well, this is how I got to know her. Well, I told you the story of me walking around New York, not knowing, waiting for something to happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Okay. At that time, where we had--where my parents had a house, they had rented a house in Crestwood, which is just outside of New York City; it's a, you know. And Bronxville is where my wife was brought up, born and brought up. Which is a few, you know, short distance away. So, when I enlisted and was waiting to be called, I was walking around and I met some guys who were also walking around like I was, waiting to be called. And several of them were down in Bronxville, were all a part of a group that my wife was part of, the high school all of them, and all the rest of the stuff that was going on; you know. So, I would visit with them and we would, together we would see--I used to tease her unmercifully at that time, when I first knew her, because she was playing soccer. And here I am growing up, you know, in England, playing soccer. And to see girls play soccer, it didn't seem to be right to me. So, I teased the hell out of her about it. But, be that as it may, we met there and we went together. And we were just friends, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you stay in touch during the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. So, during the war, you know, over time, whenever I had some leave, which was not too often but a couple of times, I would come to Crestwood were my parents were, and I would go down and we would meet and have dinner and visit all the other guys and people. So, that went on all the way until 1946. And then, I guess, we decided it was probably getting kind of difficult to keep on running around, so we decided we would get married. And then, so, we got married in May of '46. And so that's where--that's where it started.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, you were still -- you stayed in the Air Force after the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was in--well, I had a break for a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And then went back in again, in--in -- before the Korea, before Korea, about early '50. And from then on, and primarily.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. So, you were--you say you were out for a year. So, you stayed in the Air Force until about '48?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, '48--I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What were you doing then, after the war?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was, it was simply local flying. No big deal.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Where were you stationed?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was stationed in Macon, near Macon, Georgia. It was a big airfield.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And were you living in Air Force housing?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well, no. Well, we were living in a little village-type thing, little houses. We rented.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, it was civilian housing?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes, it was civilian. And it was okay. And then, when--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So decided--so, did you -- when you got out of the Air Force, what was the idea, that you were just, you were going to retire --

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- Or did you go into the Reserves?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was going--I wasn't planning to do -- I wasn't -- I thought I'd finished. No. So, that went on for a while, then I found there were things going on that interested me, and I, you know, I would do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you then get drafted to go back into the Air Force, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. No, I enlisted. I went back and enlisted, back in -- I went back and enlisted. So, I got--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: This is prior to the, or at the start of the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was '50, early '50. Yeah. Then, I went in and--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, when the Korean War started, what were you assigned to do there?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, when Korea started I was part of a--well, actually, they started me, and it also gave me a little qualifications in fighters, in F-80 fighter bombers, which was a group.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, kind of what you started out in, in World War II.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, when I started, I was--well, I mean I was flying normal aircraft, twin engines, though. But then, I got assigned to the 8th Fighter Bomber group, which was then shipped to Korea, Suwon, Korea, which I went with. And I was then assigned to the duty there. In that duty I was kind of, how shall I describe it, the most hated guy in, in the whole of the Korean peninsula, because I was the Office of the Inspector, the Inspector General's office. And my job was to see that they were working and doing the right things.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you weren't flying anymore?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was flying, but flying not--I mean, I wasn't flying combat flying. I was flying support flying; flying back to Wiesbaden -- or not Wiesbaden. Wherever the hell did we have our base back in the back; but we had our base back, and we flew back there to get our stuff, and then back to Korea.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Korea.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, that was a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you were working inspector, you weren't, you weren't flying as a combat--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- or a fighter pilot or a transport pilot?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. I was flying, just flying--I was just flying as a support pilot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: You know, carrying stuff, taking things, people someplace, or whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And working for the Inspector General?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, when you showed up everybody had to stand at attention?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right. They'd better watch out or I'd have them--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you have a white glove that you used?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. But they accused me of any number of things, however. So, I finished a year in Korea.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And from there, where were you stationed, after Korea?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Let's see. From there, I was sent back to, yeah, Warner Robins, Georgia, which a big depot and so on and so forth; an airport. And there, I was, I had a weird kind of thing, kind of junior command of support groups. It was--I got to fly a lot, a lot more than I was flying, but not, wasn't much of anything, support flying.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And my main job was in a management job for the depot, at the depot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, it was mostly a desk job?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Mostly, yeah; fundamentally desk.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: How did you get involved with the Strategic Air Command?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I never--I was not ever in Strategic Air Command.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Oh. Oh, you weren't? Okay. I'm sorry, I misspoke.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I've always--I've always been in the other kinds of Commands; from Warner Robins -- you know, when you get to be my age, you don't remember anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Well, you were over in Europe for a time.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Well, how did you end up there, and what were you doing there, in Norway.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Now, let's see. Where was I in Norway? I was in Oslo, Norway, with NATO.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: With NATO. Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yep. I was with NATO Forces, in Allied Air Forces in northern Europe. And I was the head of an evaluation group, if you will, for northern Europe. Flight of aircraft and flying from Norway, north of Norway, down to Czech Slóvakia and Germany, was my whole territory. And I would go and see that they were functioning, and as they were getting together; you know, that kind of work; kind of over-looked.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, administrative work again?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Again, administrative; and my flying was all C-47's and no, no fighters.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Were you piloting the planes as you flew from place to place?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, I--oh, yes. I maintained qualifications, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And when were you--so, when were you involved with this? This is in the '50's?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: This is--when you say this?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: In Norway, in NATO?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yes, it started--it started in the early '50's.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, it started in '50; '51.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: It's after Korea?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And during the height of the Cold War?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I came out--yeah. I came out of Korea, and then came back to Warner Robins. Then, I worked there for a while, and then shipped to Pitcher Field in New York New York; that's where I believe it was; and from there to Norway. I came back from Norway in '62? '58 to '62, I guess. Then, from there I went to Hanscom Field, up here in Boston area. That was research and development work in electronics. And I finished there and went to the Pentagon. And in the Pentagon--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What were you doing at the Pentagon?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: At the Pentagon, just head of one section of logistics.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you work with the Joint Chiefs?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, not directly, but indirectly I guess, seeing that it was working the way everything was supposed to work.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Now, at this point, Vietnam must be starting up--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, they were--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- heating up.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- yeah. Yeah, heating up.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, what was your role there?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I was -- I was not in Vietnam, I was in the Pentagon. So, I was doing the work I was doing, which was partially in support of what was needed.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: In Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you anticipate being shipped out and having to do any duty over there?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, the thought occurred to me, as a matter of fact. And--but about that time I had reached 27, 28 years. And I thought, well, I don't think I need to practice in Vietnam. But it did -- let me put it this way, it didn't appear eminent, so I didn't push it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: One thing or another. But I finally reached a point where I said, okay, enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And that's when you finally did retire?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- Vietnam was just about ending anyway, and I--so, I retired.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you retired in 1960--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: In, at end of '67, '68; '67 or '68.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And that was it. That's your military service.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, that, that took it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That did it all.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Right. And you, you didn't stay in the Reserves?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You just retired, and?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: No. I just -- well, you see, no matter how you retire, in my time, my prime, they keep you on. You have a, so to speak, hold on you for five years once you retire.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Provided, you know, you're in one piece.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And so, that didn't occur to bother me, anyway. But I retired and I went on my way. I started on my own.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay. Did you maintain any kind of interest in flying after you left the Air Force, in terms of did you fly an airplane, or did you get up in an airplane at all, do any flying?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I started, but--I started, but decided not to. Because, if you don't, if you don't fly enough, don't fly. I grew up long enough with airplanes to know that if you don't watch it, they'll bite you.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And so, my whole contention was, okay, now I had a family, I have everything going. And if I don't fly frequently, continuously, you don't have the proficiency you should have. Particularly for most aircraft these days. So, if you don't fly, don't do it. You know, people think, oh, I'll go out for an hour sometimes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah, like riding a bicycle or driving a car.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Not the same.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Doesn't work that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you have any close shaves when you were flying that you felt like this could be it?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, I had a couple with losing an engine, an engine going out. And one of them was with a Dc-3 twin engine. But it was--let's put it this way, I was close enough to everything that it was easy to put it back in, on the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: With one engine?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, with one engine. You may try flying on one engine, if you know what you're doing. And I had one with a number-three engine out on a four-engine, which is you don't notice if you just slow down. You know it. As long as it isn't a fire or it doesn't blow up, or something like that. But those are the only real, real, what you might call hair-raisers, if you will. But they weren't--well, they were hair-raisers. But other than I've had some tough low ceiling flights, having to get into some place with no visibility and things like that. Which took a lot of, how shall I say, tightening to be sure you knew what you were doing, and to watch what you were doing. That's how you can easily have a problem, go off the runway or hit something, which you see around here a lot now. These guys, they don't--forget to open their eyes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, they're flying these little private planes--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: -- and they're just not--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: It's not the way to do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, I've had one or two of those. But that was, I considered, part of the game; you know, part of what you do.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Because I flew continuously throughout the Corps, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your wife when you were having all these overseas assignments? Did she come along with you, or did she--

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, when we went to Norway, we had two children. So, we all, they all came with us. And they went to school in the American School in Oslo. And they had a good time. And we stayed there, and my wife enjoyed it. We visited. My parents, at that time, were back in London. So, we went down to see them once in a while, with what little time that you get. But there was a lot more time in that set-up than there was during the war, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: You had time off and leave, and things like that. And we took the children around and that took up a lot of the time. And subsequent to that, these were all places in which she would be with us, and the children.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: So, you weren't separated very much?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Not, not once we started--after Korea.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You were separated in a Korea.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. I was--she was at home here in New York. And, no, I was in Korea for the year. All I could get in touch with her is by phone or letter or something like that. That was about it. But other than that, where we were assigned we were also a family.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah. Norman, looking back on your military service and especially the time that you served during the the war. Well, maybe before we talk about that, let's do one other question. Do you keep in touch? Have you kept in touch with people that you served with during your time?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, for quite some time I did. Most of them now are, are--well, of about a half a dozen close ones, four of them have passed on, and two of them are, one's out -- they're all out in the west somewhere. And I periodically hear of them, but after the first few years, your life goes in different directions. They're in a different place. Now, I do periodically change, exchange a note. Periodically we have a phone call if something comes up that is common to all of us. But after you're been out of it long enough, you know, there's not much left.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Did you get involved in any Veteran's groups after you left the service?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, peripherally, but not full- time. Not like some of these people.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: To be absolutely blunt, my interests after I got out, were with other parts of the economy and in the world, and the rest of it. And there isn't much that I can get out of the Veteran's meeting except to see old friends. I don't, really don't get a thrill out of sitting there listening to them tell about the sugar bun committee and all that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: You know, it doesn't--

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: -- it's just not for me. Now, I think it's great that they provide a support for some guys that need it, who have nothing else.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: But that's not, that's not my thing. To be absolutely honest about it, aside from the corporation things that I did and do, both my wife and I head up a foundation, a charitable foundation of some size. And that just by itself is a full-time job the year round, because we give away quite a bit of money and spend quite a bit of money. So, we have to look carefully into all of that to do it properly. And that does not fit the bumbling around stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: But in addition to that, to be absolutely--again, kind of, I don't know, not much use here, but to be of use to you, is that -- that takes me in. I sit on about four or five boards in which I have some interest, in the electronics area. And I started a small company in the commuter communications area, which built up for a while and then I sold out its interest recently, a couple years or two years ago. And most of the time now is taken up with what I do in these various fields. And last but not least, I'm working on my back-hand.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: I mean, you got to watch that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: You got to watch that. That takes a whole lifetime to learn how to do well.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: That's it. And you can make friends and a lot of enemies. In other words, I mean, the few people that I served with, that I thought tremendously highly of. In fact many of I, I have utmost respect for them, and I think that they're terrific. Their kind of work is different than my kind of work.
