sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, I don't -- we -- there's none left. There are only two left now.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And they're interests are totally different than anything that I have. So, I have a whole range of new--we, as my wife and I both have a whole range of different interests, which are generated in part by the philosophical stuff, with granting, with grant work and all that, takes you into everybody's business.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure. Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And not that I think that's such a bargain, but still it's there, and my interest in electronics and stuff takes me into other technical areas. So, I get to talk some in the business world and technical world. But there isn't a minute's peace in the grant work and in this business of granting money and having this sort of thing. You get a tremendous amount of warmth and satisfactory feeling to be able to do it. But you also get, your back is a little itchy when you're watching, because you don't know whether or not that's for real. And who's at it, are they really, do they really mean what they say? Are they self- serving in what respect? Which causes, you know, it causes you concern.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, we have full days everyday. And it works fine.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Well, looking back on the military service?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And just your time in there especially during World War II and Korea, you were in two wars.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: What do you think about those days, with the remove of many, many years? How do you look back on that service and those times?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, let me say it this way: I felt that in general, the work and the management and the relationships were about as much as one could expect when you assemble something instantly like that. So, it was, there were, there were areas that I felt, gee, you know, if I had a chance I could do a little improvement. On the other hand, a lot of the guys and people that I worked with, some of them should have got hit in the head because they were really, they were coasting. But by and large a greater percentage of them felt that they were fighting for a just cause. And, as you probably already know, there are areas in which the government takes advantage of the little people. But on the other hand, I think it evens out, because a lot of the guys get paid for doing nothing. You know. So, I find that, you know, what you lose in the swings you gain in the roundabouts.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Sure. Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: If I may coin that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: And the other part of it is some of the people, guys that I work with and civilians and various things, they were tremendous people. They were really, really something that you remember. Now, I don't see them anymore. Some of them lost totally. But even so, I do remember some of the things that they had to offer. And if you're not too proud to look carefully at it, there are some things you can learn, you know. And So, I feel that everybody has--you talk with a lot of people and the first thing they tell you about is how hard they've been done by. I think that's a way of looking at it, which I think is taking advantage. I would say, of the people that I see and hear them just say that, I would like them to understand that if they didn't get taken care of, they'd get their ass in a ringer, they wouldn't be around; that they get treatment, they get handled properly. And miracles we don't expect. And it is not a private business. So, you going to do what you know, do what you have to do and do it well, and then you can afford to say whether you think it's good or not. A lot of these guys have no right saying anything. On the other hand, there are a lot of tremendous people. You know. It's a long, a very, very widespread thing. So, it's very hard to come up with a single opinion. But suffice it to say that I think that the troops do a great job.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: They really, I think, at least in those days. Now, today, the young people are coming in have expectations which are far out of sight. In my humble opinion, not enough time is spent with them getting them aimed in the right direction and lowering the guns a little bit. So they don't expect to start out as the Commanding General. They remember they're going to have to work for a living. And that has to--if there's any failing in the present situation, that's the one I would feel could do with improvement. Which is to get in there, and maybe you don't have to use a big club, but you need some weapon to open a couple of times and say, you know, pull up your socks. They expect something for nothing. I see that a lot. But, you know, hell, it's that in industry, as well. It's everywhere. The whole--unfortunately, the whole society, in the young people, are turning that way; they want something for nothing. They want to be the king or the queen, and they don't want to pay for it. So, I mean, now, you don't need this philosophy for what you're doing. But I see a lot of it. And I'm sorry that it is; and worry in wartime we would get our backside whipped because you can't do it that way. But, when I was in it, there were weak ones. But by and large everybody pulled their weight. I probably could figure a way to do it differently. So could they. Everybody has a way of doing business. So, but I--my sum of it is I have a memory that I'd like to keep.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: And it's mostly a good memory?

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you know, most of my memory of that period had a wide cross-section of things going on, and most of it--most of it, I never knew it. A lot of it I wished didn't have to do. But I recognized that, you know, it's not a social event. So, I take it for what it's worth.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: So, I have no, no regrets whatsoever.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Wiener
sp.p: All right, Norman, I think that'll do it. Thanks.

sp.speaker: Norman S. Portenoy
sp.p: Well, it's the best I can do. (End of Interview)
